text: The first official international football match was played in 1872 between Scotland and England, ending in a 0-0 draw.
Brazil is the only national team to have played in every FIFA World Cup since the tournament began in 1930.
The highest-scoring international match on record was AS Adema 149-0 SO l'Emyrne in Madagascar in 2002 (own goals scored in protest).
Pele scored over 1,000 career goals according to his own count, including unofficial friendlies.
The FIFA World Cup trophy is made of solid 18-karat gold and weighs about 6.1 kg.
Lionel Messi has won the Ballon d'Or more times than any other player in history.
Real Madrid has won more UEFA Champions League / European Cup titles than any other club.
The fastest goal ever scored in a top-flight match is credited to Nawaf Al-Abed at around 2 seconds.
The first World Cup was held in Uruguay in 1930 and was won by the hosts.
Goal-line technology was first used in the FIFA World Cup in 2014, in Brazil.
VAR (Video Assistant Referee) was used at a World Cup for the first time in Russia 2018.
Manchester United, Liverpool and Arsenal each have storied histories, but only Arsenal has gone an entire Premier League season unbeaten (the 'Invincibles' of 2003-04).
The Old Firm derby between Celtic and Rangers is one of the oldest and fiercest rivalries in football.
Football is the most popular sport in the world, with an estimated 4 billion fans globally.
The Maracana stadium in Brazil set an attendance record of nearly 200,000 spectators in the 1950 World Cup final.
The yellow and red card system was introduced at the 1970 World Cup in Mexico.
Cristiano Ronaldo is the all-time top scorer in men's international football.
The first-ever penalty kick was awarded in 1891 after the rule was introduced.
El Clasico between Real Madrid and Barcelona is the most-watched club match in the world.
Boca Juniors and River Plate share the Superclasico, one of the most intense derbies on the planet.
Diego Maradona's 'Hand of God' goal against England in 1986 is one of football's most controversial moments.
The Bundesliga has the highest average attendance of any football league in the world.
Football was originally banned in England several times in the Middle Ages because it distracted men from archery practice.
Substitutions were not allowed in the World Cup until 1970.
Spain's tiki-taka style won them three consecutive major tournaments: Euro 2008, World Cup 2010, and Euro 2012.
Hakan Şükür of Turkey scored the fastest goal in World Cup history — just 11 seconds into the third-place match against South Korea in 2002.
The term 'soccer' actually originated in England, as slang derived from 'assoc.' — an abbreviation of 'association' football.
Goalkeeper Rogerio Ceni of São Paulo FC scored over 130 career goals, more than many professional strikers.
Paolo Maldini played every minute of his 25-year professional career at AC Milan — the only club he ever represented.
The penalty shootout was invented by a German referee named Karl Wald in 1970 and was first used in competitive football in 1976.
Pelé is the only player in history to have won three FIFA World Cups, doing so in 1958, 1962, and 1970.
Leicester City's 2015–16 Premier League title was won at odds of 5000-1 at the start of the season.
The offside rule originally required three opponents between the attacker and the goal before it was changed to two in 1925, triggering an immediate explosion in goals scored.
Didier Drogba negotiated a ceasefire in Ivory Coast's civil war through sheer force of personality after his team's World Cup qualification in 2005.
Hungary's 'Mighty Magyars' were unbeaten for 32 matches between 1950 and 1954, only to lose the World Cup final to West Germany in one of football's greatest upsets.
The fastest red card in professional football history was issued after just 2 seconds, to David Pratt of Chippenham Town in 2008.
Carlos Kaiser was a Brazilian footballer who faked an entire professional career for nearly two decades by never actually playing in a competitive match.
Juventus were stripped of two Serie A titles and relegated to Serie B in 2006 following the Calciopoli match-fixing scandal.
Celtic's 1967 European Cup squad was composed entirely of players born within 30 miles of Celtic Park in Glasgow.
The ball used in the 1930 World Cup final was disputed — Argentina and Uruguay each used a different ball, so they agreed to play one half with each.
Brazil wore all-white jerseys before the trauma of their 1950 World Cup defeat to Uruguay at home prompted a complete kit redesign to the now-iconic yellow.
Socrates, Brazil's iconic 1980s midfielder, was also a fully qualified physician and wrote a philosophy column for a major Brazilian newspaper.
Luís Figo's move from Barcelona to Real Madrid in 2000 caused such fury that a pig's head was thrown at him during his first return El Clásico.
The record winning margin in a World Cup match is 10–0, scored by Hungary against El Salvador in 1982.
Johan Cruyff refused to play in the 1978 World Cup in Argentina as a protest against the country's military dictatorship — his squad reached the final without him.
The Panenka penalty — chipping the ball down the middle — is named after Czech midfielder Antonín Panenka, who used it to win Euro 1976.
Denmark won Euro 1992 despite only being invited 10 days before the tournament started, after Yugoslavia were disqualified due to the civil war.
Gerd Müller scored 68 goals in just 62 international appearances for West Germany — one of the most prolific ratios in international football history.
The 1950 World Cup had no final match — Uruguay won the tournament by topping a final round-robin group, making their victory even more dramatic.
Morocco became the first African and first Arab nation to reach a World Cup semifinal, achieving the feat at the 2022 tournament in Qatar.
The fastest goal in Premier League history was scored by Shane Long in 7.69 seconds for Southampton against Watford in April 2019.
Roberto Carlos's famous free-kick against France in 1997 defied physics — the ball initially moved a full metre outside the post before curving into the net.
Pablo Escobar's Medellín Cartel heavily funded Colombian football in the 1980s, and Andrés Escobar was murdered just 10 days after scoring an own goal at the 1994 World Cup.
Saudi Arabia defeated Argentina 2–1 in the 2022 World Cup group stage — one of the greatest upsets in the tournament's 92-year history.
Borussia Dortmund's 'Yellow Wall' (Südtribüne) is the largest standing terrace in European football, accommodating over 24,000 standing supporters.
Germany demolished Brazil 7–1 in the 2014 World Cup semifinal on Brazilian soil — a match so traumatic it became known simply as the 'Mineirazo'.
Bert Trautmann, Manchester City's goalkeeper, played the last 15 minutes of the 1956 FA Cup Final with a broken neck — and only discovered this days after the match.
The first Football World Cup trophy, the Jules Rimet Trophy, was stolen in England in 1966 before the tournament and found by a dog named Pickles.
Barcelona's La Masia academy simultaneously produced Messi, Xavi, and Iniesta — arguably the most talented trio of graduates in the history of any football academy.
El Salvador and Honduras fought the 'Football War' in 1969 — a brief military conflict that was triggered by social tensions inflamed by a World Cup qualifying series.
The 1970 World Cup ball, the Telstar, was specifically designed with a black-and-white pattern to be visible on black-and-white television screens.
Paolo Rossi was serving a ban for match-fixing when he was recalled and rushed into Italy's squad, going on to win the Golden Boot at the 1982 World Cup.

Victor Hugo Morales's radio commentary of Maradona's 'Goal of the Century' — 'Barrilete Cósmico! What planet are you from?' — is the most celebrated piece of sports commentary in the Spanish language.
The record for the most consecutive seasons in a country's top flight is held by Rangers, who played 101 straight seasons in the Scottish top division before their 2012 liquidation.
Goalkeeper Jerzy Dudek's famous 'spaghetti legs' wobble on his goal line in the 2005 Champions League Final penalty shootout psychologically shattered AC Milan's players.
Lev Yashin is the only goalkeeper in history to have saved over 150 penalty kicks in professional football.
Athletic Club Bilbao have never been relegated from the Spanish top flight and only ever sign players with documented Basque heritage.
Marta of Brazil became the first player in history — male or female — to score at five consecutive World Cups.
Porto's 2004 Champions League triumph under José Mourinho remains one of the greatest managerial achievements in European football history, built on a budget a fraction of their rivals.
The 'Battle of Santiago' at the 1962 World Cup between Chile and Italy was so violent that the BBC commentator called it 'the most disgraceful exhibition of football ever seen'.
Goalkeepers were not allowed to handle back passes from teammates until 1992, when the rule was changed to prevent time-wasting.
The fastest international goal in history was scored by Davide Gualtieri of San Marino against England in 1993 — after just 8.3 seconds, before most England fans had taken their seats.
Ossie Ardiles and Ricardo Villa moved from Argentina to Tottenham Hotspur just weeks after winning the 1978 World Cup, pioneering the wave of South American players in English football.
Roger Milla of Cameroon became the oldest World Cup goalscorer in 1990 at age 38, then broke his own record in 1994 at age 42.
Neymar's €222 million transfer from Barcelona to PSG in 2017 remains the most expensive transfer in the history of football.
Just Fontaine of France scored 13 goals in a single World Cup tournament in 1958 — a record that has stood for over 65 years.
Fiorentina's iconic purple kit was adopted by accident — a batch of white jerseys was accidentally ruined in the wash and dyed purple, and the color was kept permanently.
Corinthian FC, the English amateur club, famously refused to deploy a goalkeeper during penalty kicks — they considered it unsporting to defend a penalty, as taking one implied a deliberate foul.
Ajax's 1995 Champions League winning squad had an average age of just 23 years, making it the youngest side ever to win the competition.
The Bosman ruling of 1995 transformed football forever by granting players the legal right to move clubs for free at the end of their contracts.
Spain's La Roja are the only national team to have simultaneously held the top FIFA ranking in both men's and women's football.
Zinedine Zidane headbutted Marco Materazzi in extra time of the 2006 World Cup Final — and still won the Golden Ball as the tournament's best player.
Monaco's 2016–17 Champions League squad — built almost entirely of teenagers — knocked Manchester City out 6–3 on aggregate and was subsequently sold for over £400 million.
The record number of red cards in a single professional match is 36, in a Paraguayan league game in 2011 where both squads and coaching staffs were dismissed.
Gordon Banks's save from Pelé's header at the 1970 World Cup — diving right to scoop the ball away — was described by Pelé himself as the greatest save he ever witnessed.
Messi's first professional contract with Barcelona was reportedly written on a paper napkin because no proper contract paper was available when the director agreed to sign him.
George Best was described by Pelé as the greatest footballer he ever saw — an assessment many in Northern Ireland still hold above any other.
Karim Benzema won the 2022 Ballon d'Or at age 34 — becoming the third-oldest winner in the award's history — after years of being overlooked for France's national team.
Only one player has ever won the Champions League with three different clubs: Clarence Seedorf, with Ajax, Real Madrid, and AC Milan.
Carlo Ancelotti is the only manager to have won the Champions League with three different clubs — AC Milan, Real Madrid, and Real Madrid again across different eras.
Erling Haaland shattered the Premier League's all-time single-season scoring record by netting 36 league goals in his debut 2022–23 season with Manchester City.
The 1977 European Cup Final between Liverpool and Borussia Mönchengladbach is widely credited as the match that began an era of English dominance in European football.
Ronaldinho received a standing ovation from Real Madrid fans at the Bernabéu in 2005 after his dribbling display — an almost unheard-of gesture of respect from rival supporters.
Torino were the dominant force in Italian football before the Superga air disaster of 1949, which killed their entire first team and altered the course of Italian football history.
Nigeria's Asisat Oshoala has won the African Women's Player of the Year award more times than anyone else — six times — making her the continent's most decorated women's footballer.
Japan beat both Germany and Spain at the 2022 World Cup — two former world champions — to top a group containing some of the most storied nations in football history.
Gareth Southgate missed the penalty that knocked England out of Euro 1996, and nearly three decades later managed England to the final of Euro 2020 and Euro 2024.
The 2002 World Cup began with a seismic opening round: holders France and favourites Argentina were both eliminated in the group stage without either team advancing.
Kylian Mbappé signed a contract extension with PSG in 2022 reportedly worth €630 million over three years, making it the most lucrative contract in sports history at the time.
The first ever Premier League goal was scored by Brian Deane of Sheffield United against Manchester United on 15 August 1992 — within the first five minutes of the league's opening day.
Sevilla have won the UEFA Cup / Europa League more times than any other club — seven titles, more than twice as many as the next most successful team.
Miroslav Klose's 16th World Cup goal — scored against Brazil in the 7–1 semifinal — made him the all-time leading scorer in World Cup history, overtaking Ronaldo.
The 'Christmas Truce' football matches of 1914 took place across multiple points on the Western Front, as German and British soldiers spontaneously played football in No Man's Land.
Iceland became the smallest nation ever to qualify for a World Cup when they reached Russia 2018 with a population of just 330,000 people.
Ada Hegerberg, the first winner of the women's Ballon d'Or in 2018, declined to perform a twerk when asked by the awards host on live television, making a quiet but powerful statement.
Andrés Iniesta scored the winning goal of the 2010 World Cup Final in the 116th minute — the latest ever winning goal in a World Cup Final.
Wales qualified for the 2022 World Cup for the first time since 1958 — a 64-year gap between appearances, the longest absence for any European nation that returned.
Bayer Leverkusen completed the entire 2023–24 Bundesliga season unbeaten, also winning the DFB-Pokal — the first domestic double in the club's history.
Luka Modrić won the 2018 Ballon d'Or, ending the decade-long monopoly held by Messi and Ronaldo and becoming the first Croatian — and midfielder — to claim the award.
The Maracanã originally held nearly 200,000 fans in 1950, but safety regulations and renovations have reduced it to a 78,000-seat stadium today.
Pep Guardiola's Manchester City set the all-time Premier League points record with 100 points in the 2017–18 season — the first team in England's top flight to reach a century.
Argentina went 36 matches unbeaten between 2019 and 2022, ending the run by winning the World Cup in Qatar — their first title in 36 years.
Gary Lineker was never booked or sent off in his entire professional career — a remarkable record for a striker competing in top-level football across three decades.
Portugal's Euro 2016 win came despite the team failing to win any of their first three group stage matches — making them the only major tournament winners not to win a game in the opening round.
Napoli's 2022–23 Serie A title ended a 33-year wait and was achieved with one of the most dominant single-season campaigns in Italian football history, finishing 16 points clear.
Brazil's iconic yellow jersey was designed by a 19-year-old art student named Aldyr Garcia Schlee, who won a national competition held after the traumatic 1950 World Cup defeat.
Scotland invented the passing game of football in the 1870s — before their influence, English teams simply dribbled and kicked the ball forward in a chaotic mob.
The 1954 World Cup produced more goals than any other tournament in history, with an extraordinary average of 5.38 goals per game.
Jorginho won the Champions League, Serie A, and Euro 2020 all within the same calendar year in 2021 — an achievement no other player managed to replicate.
Eric Cantona's kung-fu kick on a Crystal Palace fan in January 1995 earned him a nine-month ban from all football and 120 hours of community service.
Liverpool's 2019–20 Premier League title ended a 30-year wait for the club and was won by a record margin of 18 points — the most dominant title campaign in modern English football.

The Corinthians of São Paulo operated as a fan-owned democracy in the early 1980s, giving equal votes to players, coaches, and staff in all club decisions — an experiment called 'Corinthian Democracy'.
Sergio Agüero's 93:20 title-winning goal against QPR in 2012 — immortalized by commentator Martin Tyler's 'Agueroooo!' — is the most dramatic moment in Premier League history.
Ronaldinho's overhead kick against Villarreal in 2004 — struck from an almost impossible angle with his back to goal — was voted the La Liga goal of the decade.
Iran's Ali Daei held the world record for international goals (109) for nearly two decades before Cristiano Ronaldo finally surpassed him in 2021.
